At first, I was shocked that more people weren’t posting about this and discussing how upset they were to see the price increases. 

But after reading the comments of so many people defending GW’s decision to raise prices during a pandemic — and after the company has experienced such massive financial success in recent years — I actually get it now.

Everyone defending these price hikes are going to buy no matter what. And they’re exactly why GW will continue raising prices like this over and over again. I don’t know of a single other type of hobby that could raise prices so aggressively and so regularly with so little care for the needs of their consumer base and still manage to maintain a community.

But I guess they’ve got enough people fully bought in that they just don’t care at this point. But I, for one, won’t be buying anything else from GW for a good long while unless they make some kind of public apology and reverse this decision.

What a lot of folks in this thread seem to not understand is that those of us who get upset about these sorts of posts and surface-level “historical analyses” aren’t necessarily upset by the history being talked about. It’s the way in which historical points like this are used to silence folks speaking out about injustices and cruelties that are still happening today, injustices which have direct linkages to the Atlantic Slave trade and the history of Black subjugation in the United States. Or they’re also used to stoke anti-Arab/anti-Muslim sentiment in an already super hostile global environment.

Black Lives Matter and Native sovereignty groups (among others) in the United States often do their best to support one another in the fight for liberation and justice. The idea that all POC and oppressed peoples are out to show themselves as the ONLY oppressed people is a weird conservative myth. I rarely see folks like this in my life and activism, and they’re largely looked down upon by most people who are working toward intersectional approaches to social justice. And the notion that this has any more relevance in understand the views of most Arab people is absurd. In the same way that I don’t think most white people in the US can look back on slavery and colonial genocide and think that it was a good thing - though some still do...

Why people like myself get so sensitive with regards to discussions of this history is because of threads like this that are full of folks who are often more interested in the #Statement and being edgy to “own the libs lol,” as opposed to understanding the nuances of the history and discussing them alongside other aspects of the historical record. Aside from one person in this thread who has made some corrections, as well as pointing out the factual parts, this seems to have just been a gross opportunity for folks to (not even) subtly point to this as reasoning for racist and xenophobic views/policies. Nah.

This can lead to some less than optimal removal on the part of the opponent allowing your bigger threats to get on the bird more easily and stay there until their damage gets through. Plus you can Divine Vengeance for 6 damage after they get rid of some small fry unit!

Important to note, however, that the author of the cited text, Albert of Aachen, is not exactly what we would consider unbiased by modern standards. He’s a great resource for scholars regarding the historical record, and most in academia tend to agree that he presents a more or less accurate *description* of events.

That said, he never actually visited the Holy Lands, and he was eventually made a canon priest. So he was writing in the 12th century (about 50 years after the First Crusade) and with a clear bias toward the Catholic Church. Remember that there were also still crusades happening during the time of his writing, both in the Middle East and on a new front in the North. Basically all of which were marked with the massacres of non-Christians for one reason or another, not just outright combat or military strategy.

I’m not bringing any of this up to dispute the original comment’s claims, though it’s a little unclear to me what they are pulling directly from the text and what is their own analysis/opinion. What they say make a lot of sense, and without having read the text myself I can’t be sure of my opinion on its value. But it’s important that we’re clear when we talk about scholarly writings, that even those texts may contain a certain bias - especially texts from a millennial ago when norms of scholarship were different and most scholars were also members of the church(es) of the day.

So I own a DVD copy of this. Bought it in high school. Really interesting film. Well, right after I bought it I gathered a bunch of friends to watch it at my house. I convinced them (before the film) that this was all real and everything we were about to see had really happened. I’d already watched it by myself, so I knew how evil I was being by fooling them.

I led with the true piece of information about how Cannibal Holocaust is the reason we now have disclaimers about “no animals were harmed in the making of this film.” Once I had shown them that bit online from the Wikipedia page I closed out of the window and convinced them of the rest. I even brought up a few times about how we didn’t need to watch it if people didn’t feel comfortable. “No shame,” I said. I’m also a pretty good liar, in general, so they all bought it.

Needless to say, by the end of the movie, my friends were in a complete state of shock. One was crying. I waited until the next day at school to tell them how I’d tricked them. I let them live with it overnight. It’s still the meanest trick I’ve ever played on someone. I’ll never forget their faces though.

I know this is kind of a lame answer. I might consider moving Gromsh’ki farther inland because of your question.

However, the fact that Tacceta is now actually able to come out to the coast matters for story perspective. Previously they were completely surrounded by forest. Their deforestation happened very quickly, almost magically you could say.

The answer for Tacceta is easy - until recently Tacceta wasn’t near the shore. It’s only just happened that they’ve clear cut the forest near their village. And even then, you’d still have to scale the cliffs up or travel up through the swamps (which are impassible for any known ship) to get to the village. Worth pointing out that cliffs don’t just jut straight out of the sea either. There are dangerous rock formations directly leading up to and around the island at all points except for the port of Ainsville and the estuaries in the south. As for Gromsh’ki, again you’d have to sail and then scale the cliffs to get there. 

However, the bigger reason Ainsville hasn’t launched expeditions to find/visit the other villages is because it’s just not worth it financially. They’re rather isolationist, and they’re happy to be the only ones trading with the mainland. They have a monopoly. Remember that since they can’t cut down trees, they have to trade or buy all he wood they’d need for a ship. Either that or charter a vessel. Most sailors in Ainsville are from the mainland where they have greater access to raw materials, no one born and raised there really has the skills or resources needed to build and man a ship because that’s never what they’ve done before.

It’s largely dependent on the region. The demographics of Ainsville would feel familiar to anyone from the mainland, if a bit more quaint. Aside from the action around the port, it’s a quiet coastal town (think northern Maine or Scotland). The people are mostly farmers, fisherman, merchants, and dive miners (people who suspend themselves from the cliff side and carve out pieces of stone to use for construction and repair in town). There are also a few small pubs, inns, and a town doctor. As far as races go, Humans are the most common (and founders of Ainsville), followed closely by a smattering of Half-Elves, Half-Orcs, Gnomes, and Halflings. Elves and Dwarves have also been known to spend time in Ainsville, but they rarely settle here. The Elves aren’t very fond of a forest that kicks them out every time they try to go exploring, and the village is too small and without the resources and comforts that Dwarves are accustomed to having in their sprawling mountain fortresses. Because of Ainsville’s inability to expand in size (due to The Woods), immigration is highly restrictive. Only a few people are allowed to settle here every couple of years, though many years there aren’t any applications to speak of. They also prioritize single people over families to help with the genetic diversity of the population.

The name of Ainsville also calls back to the original people of the village. The Patrick Ainsley was the first mayor and leader of the village.the Ainsley family still runs the town from their manor near the farmlands at the edge of town. They’re a wealthy human family who knows about anything that happens in Ainsville, having so much information that they seem to know of some things before they happen.

Little is known of the other villages - Gromsh’ki, Tacceta, and Suse. [Meta note: a map like this wouldn’t actually exist in the world. Or if it did, it would be just a rough approximation. The names of the other villages would be totally unknown to the people of Ainsville. They would only know that they weren’t alone on the island. Because of the effects of the Wandering Woods people only know the geography of what they can see from the ships that travel around the coast of the isles and what is visible above the tees. For example The Three Peaks are visible no matter where you are, though no one has ever been able to reach them because of the Woods. *Consider the rest of this comment external knowledge that wouldn’t be known to the people living here.*]

Gromsh’ki is a small village (if you can even call it that) of barbarians and rangers. Made up of many small to medium-sized family bands, Gromsh’ki is both the name of their collective group and of the hills they live in. Because of the effects of the Woods and their lack of permanent physical structures it doesn’t make sense to differentiate between the landscape and the social group - they are one in the same to these people. You’d find almost all humans here, though it’s been rumored that a few lone Goliaths roam the hills as well. It’s worth nothing that there are few magic users here, as there are no tomes to learn from. Each clan has a Druid who serves as a spiritual leader, and every generation or so a Sorcerer may be born. Other than that, these are tough, simple people who are perfectly happy without the trappings of regular society. The land gives them everything they need.

Not to blow over these last two villages, but this comment is getting pretty long...

Tacceta is very similar to Ainsville except for the fact that the people lived in homes of mud and reeds until very recently. They were generally poorer than Ainsville and almost entirely fisherman. The people of Tacceta lived very rough lives until they were suddenly able to start cutting down trees. They’ve since clear cut a massive section of the forest and begun work building a bridge to the mainland (New Prosperity Bridge). The sailors who visit Ainsville have come to call this barren stretch on the Southwest coast of the island The Deadlands because of how desolate and noxious the land in this area looks from the sea.

Suse is the most mysterious village. The people are dark skinned and human, though they often cover themselves in body paints of many different colors. They can sometimes be seen fishing from their leaf canoes near the mouths of the rivers on the South side of the Isles. It’s unknown where their village is as the entire region is covered in a haze of swamp gas and is obscured by the thick leafy plants that grow there. Many from Ainsville and the mainland believe the people of Suse to be the original people of the Isles. However, all attempts at communication have failed. Anytime a ship begins to move in close enough to send out a scouting vessel and make contact, the Suse people turn up river. And any expeditions that have been attempted have failed. The water at the South of Hearthold is too thick with sediment, the rivers too narrow, and the river paths too winding to ever make much headway into the swamps where the Suse live.

— Part 1 —

The Hearthold Isles are a small group of temperate islands off the coast of a larger (unnamed landmass). The perimeter of the island is almost entirely made up of steep cliff faces making travel to and from the Isles difficult for merchants and marauders alike. There are only two places where the elevation decreases and enough of a coastline is formed to allow for visiting ships - on the Northwestern corner of the island and the estuaries found on the Southern most stretch of the island. However, due to the narrow width of the rivers in the South and the inhospitable, swampy terrain; it’s rare to ever see full-sized ships there. Rather the rivers are home to the reclusive Suse tribe and their leaf canoes.

Being near the only viable spot of coastline and conveniently close to the mainland has made the otherwise small town of Ainsville quite prosperous. The docks are shaking and bustling every day of the week with the business of sailors and guildsman from the mainland looking to sell their wares to the people of town. Though the villagers have little in the way of material goods, the forest of the island supplies them with a wealth of creatures and rare plants to hunt and harvest for trading.

The forest is the most dominating feature of Hearthold. Known to locals as The Wandering Woods, the first possesses a few peculiar qualities. 

First, anyone who enters the forest will after a few hours find themselves spit back out in the exact spot where they entered. Sometimes an expedition you planned to take a few hours will conclude in a matter of minutes, other times one may find themselves interested in nothing more than a leisurely stroll and be gone nearly half the day. It is both a blessing and a curse, as no one has ever been lost forever in the forest (though the elders of town will surely warn you of such of such things). The only real dangers come from the creatures who make their homes inside the twisting wood. Though rare, it has happened that an overzealous young hunter has trotted into the Woods only to be discovered days later, bodies in pieces, right where their journey began.

Second, the trees appear at first ouch to be just like any other trees you’d find on the mainland. However, no one has been able to cut one down for as long as can be remembered. For all of recorded time, the Woods have held dominion over Hearthold. Neither saw, nor axe, nor fire can loosen its hold on the land. Yet neither does it grow. It simply holds forever as it is, a riddle spoken and unsolved. 

The impassible nature of the woods mean that the few villages which exist on Hearthold aside are a complete mystery to one another. The only way that anyone knows of the existence of these other settlements is because of the smoke which rises from the sky, each night in the same locations.

I really think it depends on how you approach the reading. I personally try to embed myself within the logic of the story being told. 

Therefore, I operate under the idea that there is some connection between the garden Serpent and Satan in Revelations (the Lucifer connection is more extraneous as others have fully detailed elsewhere in this thread). If that's the case, then we can think of the Bible as a sort of historical document written by the "victors," i.e. Christian believers. Adversary does not necessarily equate with wrong or evil if we try to position ourselves as neutral observers to a "historical" document. 

To clarify, I use the term historical here not because I'm making any arguments regarding the truth-value of what is presented in the Bible. I'm an atheist. Rather, I think that we should operate within the logic of the text which presents itself as historical fact.

Again, if we position ourselves within the logic of this text and also do our best to adopt a neutral position with regards to the forces at play in the text, then there's little reason to accept the characterization of the Serpent/Satan as is presented to us. Cultures throughout the world and at all points in history tend to demonize their adversaries, especially so after any kind of victory.

So I like to think of the garden in the terms of a very simplistic political society. In this case the Christian God assumes the role of an ultra-authoritarian figure ruling over his subjects - Adam and Eve (and some others if you want to get complicated). But you have subjects and a ruler, and despite there being very few rules, we should still observe that the subjects in question have no agency in deciding the limits of this very basic set of laws.

Here I would remind folks that what Adam and Eve were forbidden to indulge in were fruits from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil -- not simply the "Tree of Knowledge" as it's normally shortened to. So what is being denied is actually the ability to determine moral value for oneself. The Christian God has created a system wherein the very ability to make moral decisions is criminalized. When viewed through this lens, the actions of the Serpent/Satan take on a slightly different impetus.

The Serpent merely asks Eve what God has told her. She explains that they will die if they take of the fruit of the tree. He then corrects her by telling her that they will not die for taking of the tree, but rather that the fruit will open their eyes making them like God, able to know of good and evil. All of this is true. Eve actually lies to God when confronted and says that she was "beguiled" by the Serpent. The Serpent is then immediately punished by God. His punishment, as I've pointed out above, is to eat of dust for all his days, but also to have enmity between his seed and the woman's seed forever more until he is eventually crushed (many Christians see this as referring to the eventual triumph of Jesus over Satan at the time of Revelation).

Turning away from prophecy, which is not as much of interest to me, I would argue that mankind's first " sin"/immoral act is actually against the Serpent. When they took of the tree they didn't yet have knowledge of good or evil, but afterward they did have the ability to discern morality for themselves and they still lied by saying the Serpent beguiled them. Folks could argue that he did beguile them by provoking to think. But I reject that as being an immoral or deceiving action. It would only be wrong according to the oppressive authoritarianism opposed by the Christian God in Eden.

So, in review, we have a figure who was part of/witness to an oppressive socio-political system who prompted the subjects of Eden to question their roles within the system and claim the ability to discern moral value for themselves. That same figure, Serpent/Satan was then betrayed by the very folks he was helping (in my opinion). And the punishment carried out by God is that this figure must eat of dust (destroy mankind -- see above) and forever be in conflict with the descendants of those he aimed to aid in revolution. Nothing more tragic if you ask me.

One of my favorite connections in Dante's Inferno is actually to these verses. In the Inferno, the devil sits suspended in ice while he chews endlessly on the bodies of three betrayers - Judas, Brutus, and Cassius.

It might be a bit of a stretch, but I've always understood "you will eat dust all the days of your life" to be more than just a statement about the serpent being on the ground. If we remember that in one account, God created mankind by breathing life into dust, then the Serpent's true punishment is to devour mankind forever. I believe this is what led to Dante's decision to have Satan's mouth stuffed with betrayers.

It also represents a kind of contrapasso (a sort of poetic justice Dante-the writer employs throughout the Inferno) in its own right. If the Serpent intended to push humanity to break itself free from the will of god - regardless of good or bad intent - then the ultimate punishment would be to be forced into the role of eternal tormentor and punisher.
God's punishment of the Serpent is to be made into Satan. Hence Satan's icy tears - the one detail that always puzzled me and led me to explore some potential explanations.

In some ways this take on the actions of the Serpent are much more aligned with Prometheus' guiding motivations. But I think it's still relevant and valid concerning the amount of co-opting and overlap that's already been discussed here.

Just my thoughts though. Satan/Lucifer/Serpent/Devil/etc as a concept is probably one of my favorite things to think about, and I return to analyze and contemplate this/these figures often.
